title: EFFECTS OF INDOOR LIGHTING ON MOOD AND COGNITION
research_question: Do luminous milieus act as mood inducers, and if so, do these mood valences impair or enhance ongoing cognitive processes?

participants.description: 96 subjects (aged 18-55) per experiment, from Sweden. Gender was an additional grouping factor.
participants.recruitment: Recruited through local press and radio advertisements, paid 200 Swedish crowns (c. 30 U.S. dollars) to participate.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A chamber-room (3.9 m × 3.8 m × 2.5 m) furnished as an office, with controlled heat and humidity, neutral room coloration (off-white walls/ceiling, grey floor, green decor elements).
Experiment 1: Two illuminance levels (dim: 300 lx vs bright: 1500 lx) and two colour temperatures ('warm' white: 3000K vs 'cool' white: 4000K) at high Colour Rendering Index (CRI = 95).
Experiment 2: Two illuminance levels (dim: 300 lx vs bright: 1500 lx) and two colour temperatures ('warm' white: 2950K vs 'cool' white: 4200K) at low Colour Rendering Index (CRI = 51-58).

measures.instrument: Six general knowledge questions (recall) and 18 multiple choice questions (recognition) about a compressed text (Carter, 1982)
Recall of three 16-word lists (positive, negative, neutral affective tones) shown on a PC-screen
7-point scale evaluation of a fictitious employee on dimensions like qualifications, motivation, attitude, intelligence, etc.
Seven 5-point unipolar items (glaring, dim, soft, bright, warm, intense, cool)

mechanisms: Luminous milieu acts as a mood inducer, which in turn affects cognitive processes.
Mood-congruence hypothesis: mood valence influences memory encoding and retrieval.
Halo effect: rater bias (e.g., based on gender) influences performance appraisals.
implementation_implications: Criteria for good indoor lighting may need to be revised to account for females' and males' differential emotional and cognitive responses to lighting parameters.
Lighting design should consider gender-specific preferences and performance enhancements related to colour temperature and illuminance.

limitations: Previous studies (e.g., Baron et al., 1992) may have failed to find direct mood effects due to insufficient exposure time or incorrect timing of mood measures.

The performance appraisal task in the current study only included one gender for the ratee, limiting conclusive data on the halo effect; future studies should vary both rater and ratee genders and mood valences.

paper_metadata.title: Impacts of home lighting on human health
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Impacts of home lighting on human health
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Typical home lighting practice is mainly centred on visual aspects to enable safe movement between spaces, flexibility in multiuse spaces, a sense of aesthetics and energy efficiency. Whilst lighting impacts on the health of residents have not received similar consideration, this area is gaining increasing interest. This is even more important and actual in the context of the recent pandemic where people have been working or studying from home. A combination of bright daytime light and night-time darkness is essential for circadian entrainment and maintenance of a regular daily sleep–wake cycle, whereas exposure to light at night can negatively impact circadian rhythms and sleep patterns and ultimately lead to potential health problems. Additionally, lighting also has the potential to affect health through associated effects such as flicker, glare, optical hazards or electromagnetic fields. This article discusses the main areas of concern related to home lighting and outlines general recommendations to limit detrimental effects and contribute to good health.
